items.title: Memory management in 40 major C projects, a survey
items.content:
Memory management in 40 major C projects, a survey

A survey of 40 major C projects tracked by The Consensus shows only 8 projects allocate solely with malloc/free, only 2 projects allocate without ever using malloc/free, 15 projects make use of regions at some point, 7 projects primarily use regions to allocate, 5 primarily use garbage collection to allocate, and 3 primarily use reference counting to allocate. C Programming Languages Web Servers Compression Databases Developer Tools Operating Systems Version Control Sandboxes Machine Learning Vector Databases Apache HTTP Server Brotli Citus Emacs Erlang FreeRTOS Git HAProxy Julia LZ4 Linux Lua Neovim OCaml PHP Perl PostGIS PostgreSQL Python QEMU Redis Ruby SQLite TimescaleDB Universal Ctags Vim XZ Utils Xen Zstandard curl dqlite libdeflate llama.cpp nginx pgBouncer pgvector seL4 tmux tree-sitter zlib

Phil Eaton Artwork by Andrea Chersia Focus

You are getting early access to this article as a subscriber. Your support makes articles like this possible. Thank you. C is well known for requiring manual memory management with malloc and free. And while many major projects do actually manage memory like this, many projects also implement higher-level memory management primitives such as regions (where objects allocated within a region need not be manually freed, freeing a region frees all objects allocated within the region at once), reference counting (manually incrementing and decrementing outstanding references, freeing an object only when its references go to zero), scope-based cleanup using compiler extensions, and a number of major C projects even actually implement garbage collection (fully automatic memory management). Programmers sometimes assume that projects famous for diligence lean away from purely manual memory management. But SQLite , famous for correctness, allocates 100% manually while cURL and Redis allocate mostly manually (94% and 79%), reference counting only some of their objects. Another surprising finding is that Linux and QEMU in the last few years have been starting to use scope cleanup rules (i.e. compiler extensions) to automatically clean up memory, such as Linux's __free(kfree) and QEMU's g_autofree . The Consensus tracks and indexes code for over 400 major software infrastructure projects . This article surveys 40 of the C projects within this group, excluding test code, third-party code, and examples. Majority allocation strategy #

To discover majority allocation we count allocation call sites (which is certainly a limited metric, not accounting for sub-region or size of allocation, etc.). seL4 is an exception to much of this article since it has no heap at all. 8 projects solely allocate with malloc, implementing no other general higher-level strategy for allocating. These projects are: brotli , FreeRTOS , HAProxy , libdeflate , lz4 , SQLite , xz-utils , and zlib . 16 projects primarily, but not exclusively, allocate with malloc. items.title: Inside the Secretive, Contradictory World of Campaign Ads Funded by AI Super PACs | Bellingcat
items.content:
Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published . Become a member and support our work here .

An online ad for Ben McAdams, the Democratic candidate for Congress in Utah, emphasised that he could be trusted because he “fought back against MAGA”.

In Texas, another ad promoted Republican candidate Chris Gober, calling him a “MAGA warrior”.

What’s interesting is that both ads were ultimately paid for with money from the same organisation – Leading the Future (LTF), a Super PAC which opposes regulations that “constrain” innovation in AI. The network has received US$125 million in funding in total from OpenAI president Greg Brockman, his wife Anna Brockman, tech-focused venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and a16z’s founders, Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings show.

Directly opposing LTF is Public First Action (PFA), which calls for AI safety regulations and guardrails. PFA has received $40 million in funding from AI company Anthropic.

Like the ads run by organisations funded by LTF, the Super PACs funded by PFA also ran ads that appeared supportive or critical of Trump depending on the voters they were targeting.

As the US 2026 midterm elections approach on Nov. 3, Super PAC spending on political advertising has reportedly soared to record highs , surpassing US$11 billion last week and exceeding the amount spent on any other election cycle to date.

Super PACs are a particular type of political action committee (PAC) that may receive unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, labour unions and other PACs for the purpose of financing independent expenditures and other independent political activity.

In this year’s elections, LTF’s and PFA’s Super PACs, funded by the AI industry heavyweights, have played an outsized role in supporting or opposing candidates through advertising. But as polls show distrust of AI crosses party lines , the advertisements that Silicon Valley’s leaders are paying millions of dollars to try to sway the results in their chosen candidates’ favour often do not mention AI at all.

While LTF is a registered Super PAC itself, FEC filings show it mainly disburses money to other Super PACs in its network which run political ads.

Of about $52 million that LTF has disbursed to date , $20 million went to Think Big, which targets the Democratic voter base, and another $20 million went to American Mission, which focuses on Republicans.

PFA, meanwhile, is registered as a “social welfare”, or 501(c)(4) , organisation. This type of non-profit is not required to disclose its donors or disbursements. However, PFA contributes funds to three Super PACs : the bipartisan Public First PAC, Jobs and Democracy for Democratic candidates and Defending Our Values for Republicans. FEC filings for these Super PACs show Public First PAC received $1 million, Jobs and Democracy received $15.4 million and Defending Our Values received $7.9 million from PFA. Public First PAC’s FEC filings also show that $4 million of its $4.4 million in disbursements disclosed so far went to Jobs and Democracy, while another $300,000 went to Defending Our Values.

Super PACs are allowed to accept unlimited contributions from other political committees, and other similar networks of Super PACs have been observed in the current election cycle, such as cryptocurrency-linked Fairshake and its affiliated Super PACs .

Bellingcat analysed data on more than 300 online video ad campaigns paid for by Think Big , American Mission , Jobs and Democracy and Defending Our Values from Google’s Ad Transparency Center. These ad campaigns, many of which used the same videos in slightly different formats or across different platforms, supported or opposed 40 candidates.

items.title: Redox OS Gets Golang Working, GIMP Ported & Simplified AI Policy
items.content:
Redox OS Gets Golang Working, GIMP Ported & Simplified AI Policy

Written by Michael Larabel in Operating Systems on 14 November 2026 at 11:06 AM EST. 16 Comments

The Rust-based Redox OS open-source operating system is now out with its October development summary that highlights recent software ports, progress on NUMA, and other enhancements made to this from-scratch platform.

Redox OS in October managed to get the Go programming language compiler working on the platform. Golang on Redox OS is working both for cross-compilation and self-hosted compilation. Golang is adapted to use Relibc.

Redox OS also managed to get the GIMP image editor working after months of work. Redox OS has also updated its Servo browser engine port against the newer Servo 0.7 code state.

Redox OS has also confirmed its initial NUMA support is working nicely, fixed RISC-V dynamic linking, and implemented initial rootless package installation in user equivalent paths.

Redox OS in October also simplified its AI policy down to:

"Redox OS does not accept contributions generated by LLMs (Large Language Models), sometimes also referred to as “AI”."

More details on these enhancements plus driver and kernel improvements and more via the Redox-OS.org blog .

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임받을 이용자가 [매니저 위임 신청] 버튼으로 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 활동 중인 부매니저가 있으면 부매니저만, 부매니저가 없거나 모두 부재중이면 회원이 신청할 수 있습니다.

신청하면 갤러리 공지로 신청 글이 등록되고, 신청일로부터 7일간 찬성 댓글을 받은 뒤 운영자가 검토해 위임합니다. 첫 번째 위임 신청자가 신청한 날로부터 7일간 3명까지 동시 신청이 가능합니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 2개, 댓글 4개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 1일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

items.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
items.content:
This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.

First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.

The second reason is legal: purely AI -generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute , which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI . Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI -generated images to be tagged as Public Domain .

However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI -generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.

Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: MediEvil Is Back From the Dead on PC, and Its Developers Want AI Nowhere Near It
items.content:
Sir Daniel Fortesque has been brought back from the dead quite a few times over the years, although I suspect even he might be surprised by his latest resurrection. Almost three decades after MediEvil first arrived on the original PlayStation, a small team of developers has managed to bring the 1998 classic to modern computers, complete with improved visuals, widescreen support, modern controller features and the sort of technical improvements that weren't remotely possible on Sony's original hardware.

The project is called MediEvilRecomp, and it's being developed by a team known as BlackLabelHQ. But before you even reach the installation instructions on the project's GitHub page, there's something the developers appear particularly keen for everyone to understand. "This Recomp was made by human hands, no AI is involved in writing this code!" It's a super emphatic declaration, especially at a time when AI-assisted programming has become increasingly common in emulation, reverse engineering and homebrew development. BlackLabelHQ isn't simply stating that the project was written without generative AI. The team has established rules explicitly rejecting AI-generated contributions, and contributors who disregard those rules risk being banned from its repositories.

It's a strong position to take, although there's considerably more to MediEvilRecomp than its development philosophy. The project represents another substantial achievement for the growing community of developers finding ways to bring classic console games to modern computers without relying on conventional emulation. And for a game as wonderfully peculiar as MediEvil , there's something rather fitting about giving Sir Dan another opportunity to rise from his grave.

GitHub - BlackLabelHQ/MediEvilRecomp: Static Recomp of PSX USA MediEvil, By BlackLabelHQ

Static Recomp of PSX USA MediEvil, By BlackLabelHQ - BlackLabelHQ/MediEvilRecomp

When MediEvil arrived on the PlayStation in 1998, it was unlike most of the other games competing for attention on Sony's enormously successful console. Its hero was a skeletal knight missing an eye and his lower jaw, its world was populated by grotesque monsters, and its atmosphere borrowed as much from gothic fantasy and dark comedy as it did from conventional action-adventure games.

The game takes place in Gallowmere, where the evil sorcerer Zarok has returned and unleashed an army of undead creatures upon the kingdom. Unfortunately for Sir Daniel Fortesque, his own reputation is far more impressive than his actual military accomplishments. Celebrated as a great hero after supposedly defeating Zarok a century earlier, Dan had actually been killed almost immediately during the battle, struck by the first arrow fired. When Zarok's magic inadvertently brings him back to life, the unfortunate knight finally gets a chance to become the hero everyone already believes him to be.

It's a silly premise, and one that helped distinguish MediEvil from the increasingly crowded collection of 3D adventures appearing during the late 1990s. Beneath its gothic presentation was an ambitious action-adventure game filled with exploration, puzzles, hidden challenges and a surprisingly varied collection of weapons. Dan could wield swords and clubs, throw daggers, fire crossbows and even use his own arm as a weapon, all while working his way through graveyards, villages, haunted landscapes and Zarok's increasingly elaborate creations.

In a 2012 interview with PlayStation Blog , original designer Chris Sorrell explained that the game had initially been conceived under the working title Dead Man Dan . His original proposal combined the arcade action of Capcom's Ghouls 'n Ghosts with the visual style of Tim Burton, particularly The Nightmare Before Christmas . Lead artist Jason Wilson shared that enthusiasm for gothic artwork, and the two helped establish the game's distinctive appearance.

items.title: Software developers need an Agentic manifesto
items.content:
I can’t decide whether Agile development is completely dead or about to make a huge comeback. Or maybe Waterfall will. Who knows?

Coding agents are changing everything — and I don’t think we’ve quite figured out how they are going to update our methodology, or how we are going to organize ourselves to take advantage of them. We have barely scratched the surface.

Folks who have been around a while will remember the Waterfall method for developing software. Because coding was the hardest part of any project, Waterfall called for figuring everything out before you even started writing code. You would write a huge specification, detailing everything, then turn it over to the development team. The development team would build to the spec and pass the software on to the testing team who would verify it, and finally the project would be delivered to customers.

Never mind that by the time the thing was built and tested, what the customer wanted had probably changed dramatically. And if the customer decided they wanted a widget here and a sprocket there after the specification was written? Well, that would be a formal change request and would require a whole lot more time and money, thank you very much.

It didn’t take long for everyone to figure out that the Waterfall way wasn’t going to cut it. Projects were almost always late and not at all what customers wanted. There had to be a better way, and eventually a bunch of software luminaries quite literally got together in a room and wrote the Agile manifesto . They argued that you didn’t have to be so rigid to actually get things done. It was quite revolutionary at the time .

The Agile manifesto helped popularize methods like Scrum and other implementations of Agile, which of course have been much debated. We software developers like to kibitz about how to write software, but despite petabytes of bits dedicated to what Agile is and isn’t, we all generally agreed that Waterfall needed to be relegated to the Recycle Bin of history.

But now? I wonder. One of the reasons Waterfall was developed was that implementation was so hard — and the biggest bottleneck. Now that implementation is easy, and no longer the bottleneck , how does that change how we should develop software?

I’m going to say it has to completely change how we view the process. But how?

It might just be that Waterfall makes a big comeback. If the specification becomes the definition of the application, and the code can be generated in a trivial amount of time, would it not make sense to write a complete and thorough specification, then let the coding agent produce it in a matter of hours or days?

If coding is trivial, might we iterate on the specification rather than the implementation? In other words, how about we use the Agile methodology on the specification, updating the spec based on customer feedback and how the software is implemented by the coding agent?

What if the development process looked like this:

Have the customer agree to the specification

Build the application with a coding agent

Get customer feedback on the resulting application

Update the specification based on that feedback

Here the customer signs off on the specification changes and the implementation.

Build the application with a coding agent

Get customer feedback on the resulting application

Update the specification based on that feedback

In this version, the customer never sees the specification and only sees a working application, but you treat the specification, not the code, as the real source of truth.

Taking a step back, what the heck is this thing? You are focusing on the specification — basically getting it right before delivering the software. That’s Waterfall. But you are iterating over things and getting customer feedback along the way, and that is the basis of Agile.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.title: The MacBook Pro's OLED PWM problem
items.content:
Apple has brought tandem OLED technology to the MacBook Pro , joining the Mini-LED display that has served the range since 2021 (and which Apple continues to sell ). Apple calls this a “PROLED XDR Display”. It features individually illuminated pixels, effectively infinite contrast, wonderfully deep blacks and the sort of image quality that Mini-LED, for all its considerable strengths, can’t fully equal. Peak HDR brightness has increased, and Apple has introduced a new display engine designed to manage colour, luminance and pixel usage with extraordinary precision. And of course, in a first for any Apple notebook display, it has touch-input capability.

When Apple unveiled the new MacBook Pro, the initial reaction to the screen was overwhelmingly positive.

But there’s a burgeoning discussion taking place within the Mac community that deserves attention. On ⁠ MacRumors forums , a thread titled RIP MacBook Pro PROLED for PWM Sensitive Eyes - apple cmon! has attracted people describing remarkably similar experiences. Discussions are also appearing across Reddit, with owners describing discomfort shortly after using their new machines . Some report headaches; others describe a strange sensation of eye fatigue, dizziness, nausea, or an inability to concentrate on the screen for extended periods. Some have already returned the device .

Mike Wuerthele, of AppleInsider, published an article on 10 November titled ⁠ If you’re getting dizzy using PROLED MacBook Pro, you are not alone , examining these reports.

The following caveat probably doesn't need to be made, but I will make it anyway: these are individual experiences, not evidence that the new MacBook Pro is causing problems for everyone. Plenty of owners are likely perfectly content with (and dazzled by) their new displays. But that isn’t really the point. For the people experiencing these symptoms, the fact that somebody else can happily spend several hours staring at the same screen isn’t particularly reassuring, especially given Apple's long-standing commitment to accessibility. A display can be technically spectacular and still be a spectacularly poor display for a subset of people.

Much of the discussion centres on Pulse Width Modulation, or PWM. It’s a technique used to control screen brightness by rapidly switching or modulating the light output. On an OLED display, the pixels themselves produce the light, rather than relying on a separate backlight. By varying the way that light output is modulated, the display can control its apparent brightness.

At sufficiently high frequencies, this flickering isn’t something most people can consciously detect. But some people are particularly sensitive to this kind of modulation and can experience eye strain, headaches and other forms of discomfort when looking at displays that use it.

This is a pretty good demonstration of PWM on an M4 iPad Pro, which also has a tandem OLED display:

Neither PWM nor the discussion surrounding it is new. It’s been a talking point for years, particularly around OLED displays, and something manufacturers have increasingly had to consider as display technology has evolved (including Apple — more on this later).

Notebookcheck , which conducted laboratory testing of the 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, measured PWM at 240Hz. This is its worst-case reading, with flickering detected at brightness settings of 99% and below.

To put that into perspective, the M4 Pro MacBook Pro with Mini-LED display measured 14,880Hz in Notebookcheck’s testing. At 240Hz, the brightness fluctuation repeats 240 times per second; at 14,880Hz, it repeats almost 15,000 times per second. That’s one hell of a difference. The reported modulation frequency of the new MacBook Pro’s OLED panel is roughly 62 times lower than that measured on the Mini-LED model. [1]

items.title: 25 of my favourite modern NES games
items.content:
We are in the middle of the Second ReNESance (the first one is the one that saved the video game industry in North America). The combined decades of research and knowledge on how the venerable little NES works have produced a true cornucopia of games. We are all lucky to be here to witness it.

I am always happy to inform video game fans that the Nintendo Entertainment System is still receiving lots and lots of new third-party games.

In alphabetical order, because I refuse to rank them, here are 25 of my favourite modern NES games. Almost all can be obtained digitally, usually from the developer or publisher, most for a modest fee. Digital NES downloads are cheap! Most of these can also be obtained as physical cartridges for the true hi-fi experience on original hardware.

A little spooky, very pixelly. This game is a real gem.

Made by 8-bit Slasher who has been honing his skills in other horror games for the NES, All Hell Unleashed is an extensive love letter to the horror slashers of the 1980s and 1990s. There is an underlying story about an evil cult that is trying to resurrect something or other, but that’s just an excuse plot so that you can fight Jaws, Freddy, Jason, Ghostface and others. It works surprisingly well. You can select your favourite horror movie from a stage-select screen to do your platforming as you fight the forces of evil, culminating in the boss fights where the villain of each horror franchise swoops in for a mano-a-mano . The platforming feels good, and the boss fights function as set pieces showcasing the real villains we are here to see in their 8-bit glory.

Finally Jason dons a better outfit on the NES than that silly purple jumpsuit!

After each classic horror villain is defeated, it is time to take on the cult itself for one final showdown. Definitely a spine-tingling adventure!

Alwa’s Awakening was originally a PC game made with pseudo-NES limitations (and in the case of the music, with actual NES limitations, as the developer used Famitracker to compose all of the music). If it doesn’t feel like a classic NES game and instead plays more like a modern indie Metroidvania, that’s because it is.

In the game, you play as Zoe, a girl who likes video games and one day awakens in the mystical land of Alwa, a place from one of her games. Your task is to guide Zoe through an adventure in Alwa where she will uncover power-ups that open up new avenues of adventure. Typical Metroidvania stuff, although a bit shorter than most games in the genre. The PC-to-NES port of this game was handled by my good friend Brad Smith of Lizard fame. He made a couple of interesting YouTube videos describing the process.

The game looks absolutely gorgeous for the NES, and its Famitracker-composed soundtrack made it through the porting process completely unscathed. There was a limited physical edition that today is only available via secondhand markets. If you can grab a copy, it’s a very high-quality production. This is some of the best stuff made for the system.

Anguna is an NES game with an interesting lineage. It was originally made in 2008 for the Game Boy Advance as essentially the same game, but a bit more to the standards of the GBA. Then it was successively ported to the Nintendo DS, the Atari 2600, and finally the NES.

The Atari 2600-to-NES port was done fairly faithfully, which means that the design decisions necessary for the Atari also made it into the NES port. This means, for example, no more than two enemies per screen and always of the same type. This sort of restriction isn’t unheard of in the NES, though. The very popular NES Double Dragon port also has the same limitation. The game design makes up for it and overall results in an enjoyable experience. And isn’t that what making and playing modern NES games is all about? An interesting experience made with strict hardware limitations.

So what is Anguna? At its most basic, it’s a Zelda-like. You walk around screens, you grab new tools, your tools…

items.title: Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests
items.content:
IT-Panne Schuld für Chlorgasunfall im Phantasialand | WDR aktuell

Wegen der Microsoft-Störung am Freitag bekam das Phantasialand nicht mit, dass zu viel Chlor im Pool war. 15 Gäste wurden verletzt.

Diesem Problem waren wir alle ausgesetzt: Am Freitag gab es eine Störung, die den US-Softwarekonzern Microsoft lahmgelegt hat. Unter anderem das E-Mail-Programm Outlook.

Betroffen war auch das Phantasialand. Durch die Störung kamen keine Mails an, wie das Unternehmen dem WDR am Samstag mitteilte. So bekam niemand mit, dass das Wartungssicherheitssystem der Saunalandschaft längst per Mail Alarm geschlagen hat. Denn das automatischen Dosiersystem hatte zu viel Chlor in den Pool gepumpt.

Dadurch wurden Gäste im Hotel Ling Bao des Phantasialands in Brühl verletzt. Sie haben über gesundheitliche Probleme geklagt, nachdem sie den Pool besucht hatten. Der wurde zeitweise gesperrt, konnte inzwischen aber wieder freigegeben werden, wie die Feuerwehr am Samstag dem WDR mitteilte.

Wegen der Beschwerden der Hotel-Besucher wurden Rettungskräfte und die Feuerwehr gerufen. 13 Gäste klagten über Reizungen der Atemwege, letztlich stieg die Zahl der Betroffenen auf insgesamt 15.

Zunächst hieß es, dass fünf Gäste ins Krankenhaus gebracht wurden, später wurde die Zahl auf vier korrigiert, eine Person davon blieb wegen einer mittelschweren Verletzung zur Beobachtung im Krankenhaus.

Im Hotel ergaben Tests der Einsatzkräfte einen Defekt des automatischen Dosiersystems für den Pool. Dies hatte zu einem deutlich überhöhten Chlorgehalt geführt. Das Wasser wurde daher ausgetauscht.

Verletzungen durch Chlorgas im Phantasialand

Birgit Reckersdrees, Direktion Marketing und Sales Phantasialand

items.title: cursor:pointer on buttons
items.content:
Published on: November 13, 2026 Categories: CSSWG  8 , CSS  96 , Opinion Current music: Envy  —   Connected Voice

Three weeks ago, at a CSS Working Grouping meeting, we discussed an issue “ Cursors for base appearance ” , and resolved on the following:

The CSS Working Group just discussed [css-forms-1] Cursors for base appearance, and agreed to the following:

RESOLVED: Adopt cursor rules in the last comment.

SUMMARY: Pointer = “click this thing”, text cursor says “prepare to enter text”, grabbing hand says “drag this”.

One of the rules from the “last comment” mentioned there is

select , option , input [ type = checkbox ], input [ type = radio ],

button , input [ type = button ], input [ type = submit ], input [ type = reset ], input [ type = color ], input [ type = image ], :: file-selector-button {

Or, if we were to remove all non-button selectors,

That is, of course, not a change to the default styles in the browser — this is a rule for elements that will have an  appearance: base-… .

Also note that, this user agent style will be very much overrideable — no  !important .

Anyone who does not like cursor: pointer on buttons and other similar elements, are free to override it to  default (or anything else) in their stylesheets.

The rest of us can, I guess, celebrate? I was always on the side of this decision. I published my  “ Correct Cursor on Active Elements ” article in 2013. In 2017, I opened my first CSSWG issue — “ Change the pointer cursor to indicate any interactive element ” , which led to a change in a non-normative part of the spec.

Since then, I did not see any new arguments in this debate. I will not repeat everything that I argued about, but one of the most common counter-arguments that I read today is “OS does not do it”.

Did you see that “OS”? When was the last time your OS innovated anything in the UI? Did it become easier to use over years?

Many of people with this argument ask, thinking that this will be a good question, something like “What next — change the cursor in the OS?!”.

I mean… Yes? I would be happy with that. When I look at like half of the (non-native) apps in my desktop OS, they have cursor: pointer on interactive elements.

Cinny, Discord, Signal, Slack, Steam, VS Code — some of the apps that I have before me.

When I use apps that do not change the cursor to anything other than default , I cringe.

Default cursor does not communicate anything. It does one job well — point at a specific pixel. It could do more.

In the issue, many people came with dislikes and their arguments against cursor: pointer . I want to aknowledge one argument that I fully agree with — it would be great if buttons and links would have different cursors. And also, regular links should have cursors different from the links that are opened in new tabs.

But if we were to look at those three things:

And then had only two cursors to assign to all of them, I know which ones I will assign to which.

And I will never understand anyone thinking that buttons have more in common with blank space than with links.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Day 11 - Finding things
items.content:
Today we’ll look at how you find files, and text inside these files, quickly and efficiently.

It can be very frustrating to know that a file or setting exists, but not be able to track it down! Master today’s commands and you’ll be much more confident as you administer your systems.

Find all files that have the word “Permission” in it

If you’re looking for a file called access.log then the quickest approach is to use “locate” like this:

(If locate is not installed, do so with sudo apt install plocate )

As you can see, by default it treats a search for “something” as a search for “*something*“ . It’s very fast because it searches an index, but if this index is out of date or missing it may not give you the answer you’re looking for. This is because the index is created by the updatedb command - typically run only nightly by cron . It may therefore be out of date for recently added files, so it can be worthwhile updating the index by manually running: sudo updatedb .

The find command searches down through a directory structure looking for files which match some criteria - which could be name, but also size, or when last updated etc. Try these examples:

The first searches for files with the name “access.log”, the second for any file under /home with a last-modified date in the last 3 days.

These will take longer than locate did because they search through the filesystem directly rather from an index. Also, because find uses the permissions of the logged-in user you’ll get “permission denied” messages for many directories if you search the whole system. Starting the command with sudo of course will run it as root - or you could filter the errors with grep like this: find /var -name access.log 2>&1 | grep -vi "Permission denied" .

These examples are just the tip of a very large iceberg, check the articles in the RESOURCES section and work through as many examples as you can - time spent getting really comfortable with find is not wasted.

Rather than asking “grep” to search for text within a specific file, you can give it a whole directory structure, and ask it to recursively search down through it, including following all symbolic links (which -r does not).

This trick is particularly handy when you “just know” that an item appears “somewhere” - but are not sure where.

As an example, you know that “PermitRootLogin” is an ssh parameter in a config file somewhere under /etc, but can’t recall exactly where it is kept:

Because this only works on plain text files, it’s most useful for the /etc and /var/log folders. (Notice the -i which makes the search “case insensitive”, finding the setting even if it’s been entered as “Permitrootlogin”

You may now have logs like /var/log/access.log.2.gz - these are older logs that have been compressed to save disk space - so you can’t read them with less , or search them with grep . However, there are zless and zgrep , which do work, and on ordinary as well as compressed files.

It’s sometimes useful to know where a command is being run from. If you type nano , and it starts, where is the nano binary coming from? The general rule is that the system will search through the locations setup in your “path”. To see this type:

Try this for grep , vi and service and reboot . You’ll notice that they’re typically always in subfolders named bin , but that there are several different ones.

The -exec feature of the find command is extremely powerful.

But “finding things” can go so much further than that! You can not only track down the content of a file, but also its usage with commands like lsof and fuser .

Test some examples of this from the RESOURCES links.

items.title: A NES emulator written in Odin
items.content:
I’ve started this project in late June of 2024. I’ve worked on it in my spare time off and on. I decided to put a pause on this project in January 2025 to focus on other things.

The NES architecture, and possibly about game console architectures in general

Bits and bytes, hex notation, and bitwise operations.

The Odin programming language. I haven’t used it on a serious project before.

How computers work. CPU instructions, “cycles”, etc

Emulation. It’s very hard. Respect to emulator developers!

It’s been a wild ride. I’ve had a lot of fun, but I’ve also suffered more towards the end, when trying to make the emulator “fully” accurate.

You can read the Github Readme for more info about the project.

Enough emulation accuracy to run Battletoads and hundreds of other games perfectly.

Debugger view with some debugging features

Supported Mappers: NROM, MMC1, UXROM, CNROM, MMC3, GxROM, AxROM

I’ve seen some people say that making a NES emulator is a simple weekend project, and I frankly found that baffling. Because evidently , it’s not. It took me 7 months to get my emulator to how it is now.

I think what they actually mean is that getting a NES emulator “working” takes a short time. Like maybe getting Donkey Kong to run. And that’s true. You can get to 80% or maybe 90% pretty fast. It’s the last 10% that takes a long, long time.

The NES hardware has many idiosyncrasies that need to be emulated for certain games to run. Many games depend on very specific NES behavior. And if you don’t implement it right, they won’t run. A lot of the challenge is about timing. The CPU and the PPU (the chip that handles the graphics rendering in the NES) run in parallel and they communicate with each other. That timing needs to be very accurate, or many wrong things can happen. Most games will run fine with a less than accurate emulator, but a lot of them won’t, and they will need you to consider things in more detail.

Another issue is mappers . Mappers are what we call an implementation of a type of cartridge. You see, NES games come in cartridges, and cartridges aren’t just data. They are circuitry with their own behavior and extra resources like read-only memory, and writable memory. Some come with extra audio capabilities, but I haven’t implemented that.

Anyway, you have to implement these mappers if you want a game that comes in that cartridge to run in your game. They complete the NES’s circuitry. In a way, they are a part of the NES hardware. There are many mappers, but you can support a lot of games by just implementing a few. I’ve had trouble implementing some mappers, and some of them are still badly implemented, causing some games to not work. I found it hard to understand some of the mapper documentation.

The biggest challenge with making an emulator, I think, is to know what to implement. Information about the hardware, and what needs to be emulated about the hardware for games to work in your emulator. Thankfully, the NES is very well documented online. I’ve used many resources, like:

The nesdev wiki discord . People here have helped me with my issues a lot.

Javidx’s NES series . The code has many mistakes but it’s a good starting point.

Test ROMS . These NES ROMS thoroughly test particular aspects of your emulator. This is an extraordinary tool to accelerate development of emulator accuracy.

I wouldn’t have been able to do any of this without these resources and the help from people in the nesdev discord.

I’ve learned a lot about Odin while making this project. I think it fit this project like a glove. Being a very simple, strongly typed C-like language that gives me all the freedom I want makes making an emulator much easier than using other languages, I feel.

One thing that threw me off was that Odin has no automatic integer promotion . When doing calculations on numbers, Odin will never promote types to a bigger one. That led to a few bugs. But I blame this all on me and me being used to C’s integer…

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. items.title: Librem 5 second-gen $1599 RISC-V Linux phone - OMG! Ubuntu
items.content:
Purism is crowdfunding a new version of its Librem 5 Linux smartphone, this one powered by RISC-V rather than Arm.

Librem 5 v2 will use an octa-core SpacemiT K1 RISC-V SoC 1 , replacing the quad-core Arm64 NXP CPU. This processor shift will provide better performance and longer battery life than the original Librem 5 and not run as hot in use.

Memory is bumped to 8 GB RAM, up from 3 GB, and storage leaps to 128 GB from 32 GB. Librem 5 v2 will run PureOS , Purism’s Debian-based operating system using Phosh as its UI.

SD card read speeds are faster, which is handy since the device can boot a second OS from a memory card. On-board hardware encoding means the Librem 5 will be able to take 13 megapixel photos and shoot high-definition video for the first time.

Librem 5 v2 uses the same case design, 5.7-inch (720×1440) IPS TFT display and removable 4500mAh battery as the first handset. It retains the USB-C port, audio jack and physical kill switches to disable camera, modem and GPS.

Why no design upgrade? Intentional; compatibility with the first model makes repairs and upgrades between generations easier.

Modular wireless boards are used, with the v2 handset offering an improved 4G modem (a 5G module is planned, which can be swapped out). But the v2 will be dual SIM, whereas the v1 is single-SIM.

“RISC-V is the future, and Librem 5 v2 is the perfect product to bring it to a mainstream audience”, Jonathon Hall, CTO at Purism, says of the launch.

“Freeing us from the control of Big Tech starts with the foundation, and RISC-V’s foundation frees us from the oligarchy. The Librem 5 v2 puts you in control of your data, combining that with the ease of use we expect in the modern era”.

Given that general feedback to the first-gen Librem 5 – beset by delays, price rises and patchy build quality – was mixed best. But, to it credit, Purism is still out there making, selling and supporting the phones (and their other devices and services).

Transitioning to RISC-V for the follow-up won’t be trivial, mind. Graphics acceleration, new drivers and power management (which on a phone is rather critical) will be big undertakings.

And more work is needed to make the day-to-day software stack editable, like browser performance (sluggish on the newest and fastest RISC-V chips) and providing an Arm app compatibility layer to run software not made for RISC-V.

If you’ve got at least $1599 burning a hole in your pocket and you don’t need anything to show for it before 2028, you can go pledge to the campaign . It runs until February 2027, so don’t feel pressured to decide just yet.

Which is not RVA23 baseline; that’s K3 and up. ↩︎

items.title: A datetime library for Rust
items.content:
Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the

pit of success . Jiff automatically handles many common problems related to

daylight saving time by putting time zone handling front and center into the

API. Jiff has already seen widespread adoption in the Rust ecosystem.

Jiff is pronounced like “gif” with a soft “g,” as in “gem.”

This blog announces the Jiff 1.0 release by giving a tour of its API.

Target audience : Rust programmers who need convenient datetime handling.

Locale Sensitive Formatting via ICU4X Integration

Jiff is already used in production in many projects: uv, Cargo, Starship, fd,

Nushell, mise, Jujutsu, uutils/coreutils and even as the basis for a Temporal

implementation in AWS LLRT. It is time to call it 1.0.

Unless some significant defect is found in Jiff’s API, my plan is to commit

to Jiff 1.0 indefinitely. This is important because the intent is for Jiff

to be an ecosystem building block that appears in the public API of other

libraries. This makes Jiff an attractive public dependency, which means

semver incompatible releases are likely to cause significant pain in the

ecosystem. They will not be made lightly.

To see a list of breaking changes between Jiff 0.2 and Jiff 1.0, please

In programming, a datetime library’s core functionality rests at the

intersection of a computer system’s concept of time and a human’s concept of

time. The prevailing notion of system time is Unix time . A human’s concept

of time is far more complex, but the most popular such model is the Gregorian

calendar coupled with either a 12-hour or 24-hour clock. At the core of every

datetime library rests some routine for converting between these concepts.

A datetime library typically provides much more than this. Indeed, datetime

handling has historically been very difficult . My own belief is

that the difficulty comes from poor modeling of the domain . Instead of

encapsulating the complexity inside a reusable bundle of code, many datetime

libraries pass some or all of the complexity on to its users. Jiff instead

tries hard to encapsulate the complexity and make it difficult for users to

do something wrong. ( Jiff is not the first to do this! )

In this section of the blog, we’ll do some very basic introductions.

To follow along with the examples in this blog, create a new Cargo project

Most examples are a complete self-contained Rust program. Just copy the code

and replace whatever is in src/main.rs . Then run the program:

I am loath to present a dictionary. However, the datetime domain is littered

with confusable terms, so I think it’s important to orient ourselves on a

shared vocabulary. I’ve kept this section as small as possible. (Some terms,

like “time zone,” are omitted here because they are best defined through

exploration in the sections that follow.)

Civil time : The time you see on your clock. And in general, the time that

the humans in your approximate geographic vicinity also see. That is, civil

time is a human coordinated agreement for communicating time in a particular

geographic region. Civil time is also known as: local time, plain time, naive

UTC : An abbreviation for Coordinated Universal Time ; it is a time

standard that serves as the basis for civil time around the world. It was

originally intended to roughly correspond to mean solar time .

TAI : An abbreviation for International Atomic Time ; it is a time standard

as measured by atomic clocks. It isn’t directly connected to mean solar time.

Leap second : An adjustment to TAI to bring it closer to mean solar time

Unix time : UTC, but ignoring leap seconds.

TAI and leap seconds won’t be a feature of this blog, but they are listed here

in order to convey the difference between Unix time and UTC.

of its datetime types like an onion. In reverse order, we can build up

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Microsoft Word Changes Could Break Formatting in Older Documents Starting December 2026
items.content:
Microsoft is retiring several legacy Compatibility Mode settings in Word for Windows and Mac, a change that could affect the formatting and layout of older documents.

According to Microsoft 365 Message Center advisory MC1551147 , the company aims to simplify document layout handling and improve consistency across platforms.

The retirement will begin in December 2026 for Windows and May 2027 for Mac.

Microsoft Word Compatibility Mode Changes Could Affect Older Documents

Compatibility Mode helps Microsoft Word preserve the original formatting and layout of documents created in older versions of the software.

Microsoft plans to remove several legacy settings, although it has not disclosed exactly which options will disappear.

As a result, documents created or saved using Word 2010 or earlier could experience formatting changes, including text reflow, altered paragraph spacing, different page counts, and images or shapes moving to other positions or pages.

Organizations that maintain older documents, templates, and business records could face the greatest impact, particularly when they need consistent formatting across multiple Word versions.

When Will Microsoft Remove These Word Settings?

Microsoft plans to begin retiring the legacy settings in Word for Windows in December 2026, followed by Word for Mac in May 2027.

The announced rollout schedule specifically covers GCC, GCC High, and DoD environments. Microsoft has not clarified whether the retirement will also affect personal Microsoft 365 subscriptions or other enterprise customers.

The company has also not published a complete list of the compatibility settings it intends to remove.

Microsoft Recommends Saving Older Documents as PDF

Microsoft recommends exporting older Word documents to PDF to preserve their existing appearance and layout before the changes take effect.

This approach can help organizations retain the original formatting of important documents, although PDF files will not offer the same editing flexibility as Word documents.

Users and IT administrators who rely on older Word templates should also review their documents for potential layout changes.

In other Microsoft news, LibreOffice recently improved Excel and PowerPoint compatibility through its latest update.

Meanwhile, Microsoft’s November updates fixed USB audio issues in Windows 11 , but KB5132061 also broke Windhawk mods , prompting a temporary workaround.

items.title: Struggling to spell ‘male chauvinist pig’? Apple’s grey list means your iPhone won’t help you
items.content:
The swipe-type-thwarting list was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman. Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters

The swipe-type-thwarting list was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman. Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters

Struggling to spell ‘male chauvinist pig’? Apple’s grey list means your iPhone won’t help you

There are more than 100,000 words and phrases that the tech giant has restricted its predictive text from completing, research shows

“Australia is a very bad place to question your sexuality on MDMA with NSA spies” might be a text you would wish to send to your friends, if you have had an extraordinarily complicated night out in Sydney.

But your iPhone won’t help you spell any of it if you try to swipe-type it – that is, by gliding a finger across a keyboard as opposed to pecking out a word.

New research shows that Apple has a “grey list” of more than 100,000 words and phrases that it has restricted from being completed by its predictive text.

So if a user wishes to type phrases such as “Dictator Trump”, “NSA spies” or, surprisingly, “Australia is a very bad place”, “question your sexuality” or “on MDMA”, they will have to spell them out.

Apple’s predictive text will not suggest these words. And, if a user attempts to swipe-type them, they will often stumble, changing “United Ireland” to “United Iceland”, for example, or “Tibetan independence” to “Tibetan independences”.

The “grey list” was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman, whose other projects include using AI to find errors in scientific papers. After noticing that he had problems typing certain phrases – but not others – on his iPhone, Kauffman was able to unearth a table containing the list, encoded in Apple’s operating system.

The list he found includes some unsurprising words and phrases. Apple’s iPhone will not autocomplete references to drugs, sexual acts and, perhaps in the spirit of corporate protection, “iMessage isn’t working”.

But it also includes possibly politically charged phrases, which Kauffman described to Reuters as a “light-touch form of censorship”. Among these are “Trayvon Martin”, the name of the Black teenager shot in Florida in 2012, “Kashmir dispute”, “Muslim extremist” and “male chauvinist pig”.

In Hebrew, Apple will not autocomplete the phrase “the occupied territories”. In Arabic, it will not autocomplete the phrase “the Hamas movement”.

The list is one more glimpse into the dark bowels of how autocorrect – the chirpy keyboard partner that helps you look more educated to your loved ones – actually works.

The technology has taken many forms. In its earliest version, Unix, an operating system, would look up each word a user typed against a table of words, to determine if this word was spelled correctly.

Apple warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in memory chip prices

This evolved into n-grams, a tool which allows an operating system to statistically predict what words might come next, based on the words before it. These form the basis of Apple’s familiar autocorrect , which was known to change expletives into prudish alternatives: “fork” and “ducking”, among other gaffes.

Last year, Apple launched a new autocorrect – a “transformer-based” system that was more akin to an LLM. Reddit sleuths saw this as a possible reason behind a spate of avant-garde spelling suggestions their iPhones made last year.

This hard-coded list illuminates one longstanding mystery behind the world’s spelling coach. Others remain, such as a brief glitch in which users of the dictation feature saw the name “Trump” flash across their screen when they spoke the word “racist” into their iPhones – which Apple quickly remedied.

Apple said that it designed its keyboard to avoid offering inappropriate or offensive predictive suggestions. It said iPhone users could always type out specific words or phrases, and override predictive text suggestions to achieve their desired meaning.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
items.content:
Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs

The Methods Behind How LLMs Represent Token Positions

This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings.

Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms.

Figure 1: A preview of the gallery’s 2026 architectures, grouped by positional encoding. Architecture figures taken from my LLM gallery .

But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis.

Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover

what methods are used by recent open LLMs.

Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) . If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher:

Understanding and Coding Self-Attention, Multi-Head Attention, Causal-Attention, and Cross-Attention in LLMs

The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style.

PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses.

PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, Positional choices in modern architectures .

Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the web view here , which also has a navigation bar on the left side.

1. Where position information enters an LLM

Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token.

items.title: Federal Judge Rejects Memory Makers’ Defense To Advance Class-Action Antitrust Lawsuit; Samsung, Micron & SK hynix Must Face The Music Over Artificial DRAM Shortage
items.content:
Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron were already in the crosshairs of a U.S. federal class-action lawsuit that claimed the big-three DRAM manufacturers were involved in collusion to artificially limit memory supply  and enjoy heaps of profits. Unfortunately for these technology giants, wiggling their way out of this situation isn’t an option, as a federal judge in California has cleared the way for the antitrust lawsuit. Assuming a court order not only fines the memory makers but makes it mandatory for supply to keep pace with demand, there’s potential for this crisis to end, resulting in DRAM prices finally stabilizing.

In a ruling issued on November 14, LitNews  reports that U.S. District Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California denied Samsung’s, Micron’s, and SK hynix’s joint motion to dismiss in full, finding that the complaint plausibly alleged an illegal agreement in violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The lawsuit was filed on June 25, 2026, by 17 consumers and small businesses across five states against the trio, stating that these DRAM behemoths collectively controlled more than 91 percent of global DRAM revenue as of the third quarter of 2025.

While the defendants argued that their calculated moves were reactionary to the booming AI demand and mirrored a previously dismissed 2018 lawsuit, Judge Wise disagreed, stating, “The Court finds that it is not.” Addressing the companies’ defense that competitors in concentrated markets naturally watch one another closely, she wrote, “But Plaintiffs’ allegations go beyond hawks watching each other; their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation, an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.”

According to the complaint, the three manufacturers began cutting conventional memory production in late 2022 and redirected wafer capacity toward High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) in 2023. This allocation shift drove conventional DRAM prices up by an eye-popping 697 percent over just an 18-month span without any of the companies expanding output. Since HBM requires three to four times more silicon wafer area per GB than standard DDR5 memory, the shift severely tightened consumer and PC supply, creating clouds of misery for the entire industry.

Judge Wise did find that there were several coordinated actions executed beyond ordinary market behavior that would be difficult to reverse without a prior understanding. More specifically, Samsung and SK hynix refused long-term contracts (LTAs) with major conventional DRAM buyers, while also delaying or halting new DRAM fabrication plants. Furthermore, the three firms wound down DDR4 production in the same quarter of 2025, along with Micron’s December 3, 2025 announcement that it would be shutting down Crucial , its 30-year-old consumer memory brand.

The court also noted near-identical customer-vetting practices adopted by Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron in January 2026, alongside their price-fixing history observed between 1998 and 2002. Due to these practices, Judge Wise has ordered all three DRAM manufacturers to file their formal answers to the complaint by December 7, 2026, with an initial case management conference scheduled for January 12, 2027. You can check out the entire lawsuit document here  and let us know what you think in the comments.

items.title: Developer's $300 Embroidery Machine Required a Subscription, So She Built This Open Source Tool
items.content:
A tinkerer, Kathy Korevec , has made ZigZag available under the Apache 2.0 license. She says that the entire app was built with AI, using ChatGPT, and her goal was to get software made to her specs, similar to the Adobe suite, but with MCP support built in.

That MCP support is a built-in server that lets AI agents draw and edit in the same window.

Her post about this on Hacker News has already managed to reach top 10 status ( over a 48-hour period ), and she has been answering questions there about how this was built and which machines it supports.

This was built around a Brother Skitch PP1 embroidery machine that she says cost her around $300.

You see, the Skitch needs Brother's Artspira app to operate. While the app is free and works with the machine, a paid plan called Artspira+ adds useful extras such as digitizing images into embroidery patterns and creating cross-stitch patterns.

Kathy says the free version is limited in colors and tools , and she believes some of the clip art is reserved for subscribers. She also guesses Brother sold the machine at a loss at first because of the subscription.

That last bit checks out, seeing what many hardware manufacturers are doing.

ZigZag imports SVG art and can trace PNG and JPEG images into shapes. It covers 11 stitch types , including fill , satin , and appliqué , with a preview of the stitches being shown in the editor.

As for the MCP server , it lets an AI agent inspect the open design, add and edit objects and text, trace images, preview the stitches, and export files. It can also control a Skitch device, and each action counts as one undo step.

Open source embroidery tools existed before ZigZag. People have brought up projects like Ink/Stitch , an Inkscape extension, and Respira already lets people send designs to the Skitch without Artspira.

The project also credits Respira for the Bluetooth protocol and sewing flow. Kathy says she reverse-engineered the protocol herself and that her agent used Respira to verify it.

Currently, ZigZag is available for Windows and macOS . You can grab the latest release from the project website or its GitHub releases page .

The README covers installation, Bluetooth pairing, and the MCP server, and it advises against firmware updates on the Skitch. Linux users can follow its steps for building ZigZag from source with Rust.

The Brother Skitch PP1 is the only machine ZigZag sends designs to over Bluetooth, and Artspira needs to be closed first since the Skitch can only talk to one app at a time.

For other machines, ZigZag can export PES , DST , EXP , JEF , or VP3 files.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.
